notes: Purpose: agree on a database merge policy and a reproducible filtering policy. This deck advocates removing exact sequence redundancy while keeping biological identity and explicit project exceptions. It does not assert a measured FDR effect.
text: What should a contaminant FASTA change?

One sequence → one search record.
Project policy decides what gets excluded.

title: The reported 117 drops are fully explained
notes: Original input contained 20,430 human records and 169 Tenzer records. There were 117 extra records by accession: 116 cross-source collisions and one repeated P38507 within Tenzer. Every accession collision had an identical sequence. Header strings alone concealed most collisions.
text: The reported 117 drops are fully explained
All 117 accession-collision pairs have identical sequences.

title: A different name does not create a different ID
notes: These are actual P02538 header tokens. The middle pipe-delimited field is the accession, and remains P02538 in both records. The CONTA suffix changes the protein name. Default DIA-NN behavior keeps the first record for a repeated ID. Renaming the accession would avoid an ID collision but would still leave sequence redundancy.
text: A different name does not create a different ID
[1] DIA-NN documentation: accession parsing and default duplicate-ID handling.
Changing the ID would fix parsing; identical peptide evidence remains.

title: Two labels cannot distinguish biological origin
notes: This is a statement about identifiability from sequence evidence, not about whether contamination is likely. The measured abundance can be a mixture of endogenous and exogenous molecules. Origin requires contextual evidence such as controls; a second database label cannot supply it.
text: Two labels cannot distinguish biological origin
Schematic reasoning: identical sequences yield the same peptide candidates under the same digestion settings.
Origin may be sample, handling, or both. A suffix cannot resolve it.

title: The disagreement contains two separate questions
notes: Both concerns are valid. Removing an exact sequence copy is a database representation decision. Excluding an identified sequence from downstream analysis is a project interpretation decision. Keeping two labels is not a substitute for specifying a filtering rule.
text: The disagreement contains two separate questions
[2] Hao et al. discuss sample-specific contaminants and biological relevance of keratins.

Why search two copies of an identical sequence?

Retain one representative; preserve both sources and aliases.

Could this keratin be relevant to the sample?

Yes. Membership in a contaminant list is not proof of origin.
Deduplication and exclusion need separate, explicit rules.

title: One search result can support different project policies
notes: These are hypothetical examples, not a claim that every keratin should be excluded in a standard project or retained in an epithelial project. Both projects see the same identified sequence and contaminant-candidate annotation. Their saved policy differs. Retaining a candidate does not prove it is endogenous.
text: One search result can support different project policies
Illustrative policies only; each project must justify its own exclusions and exceptions.
Shared annotation: P02538 / KRT6A / common contaminant candidate

Handling keratins excluded.
No exception for P02538.

Outcome: exclude from analysis.

Keratin biology is in scope.
P02538 explicitly allowlisted.

Outcome: retain for analysis.
Store the decision in project config; do not rely on memory.

title: Contaminant groups can make exceptions manageable
notes: This grouping scheme is a proposal for the group to review, not an implemented or universal standard. A sequence may be a member of multiple groups. Accession overrides should take precedence over group exclusions, and the effective policy should be exported with results.
text: Contaminant groups can make exceptions manageable
Proposed taxonomy. Groups may overlap; none establishes the origin of a particular detection.

title: A merge policy must distinguish three cases
notes: The first rule is the requested example: drop the human copy and retain the contaminant representative of an identical sequence. Alias mapping preserves all original identities, including identical sequences from different genes or loci. Same accession with different sequences requires distinct record identifiers or explicit review; choosing the longest is not generally justified.
text: A merge policy must distinguish three cases
Proposed rules; sequence equality means full amino-acid sequence equality, not shared peptides alone.
One sequence record; retain all aliases / genes.
Warn; preserve both with unambiguous IDs.
Do not collapse distinct sequences solely because IDs or lengths overlap.

title: Make the policy reproducible from FASTA to results
notes: This is a proposed end state. Keep downloaded source databases intact. Canonicalize identifiers for comparison without erasing their source labels. Save sequence-to-alias mapping and decisions. Apply a versioned project policy to retained identifications. The unmodified results should remain available for reanalysis.
text: Make the policy reproducible from FASTA to results
Deliver results + effective exclusion policy + merge / alias manifest.

title: FDR is a caveat, not the central argument
notes: No before/after search experiment in this work measured a change in protein FDR or identification sensitivity. Duplicate accessions and identical sequences are distinct issues. Inference software can select representatives or group redundant records; two entries need not be counted as two independent protein discoveries. Avoid asserting an inevitable or quantified FDR penalty.
text: FDR is a caveat, not the central argument
[1] DIA-NN documentation and issue #1140: grouping and representative selection depend on inference.

Exact copies add no distinct sequence evidence.

Duplicate IDs trigger DIA-NN skipping.

Two entries may be grouped or represented by one protein.

Two entries ≠ two independent findings.

A change in FDR or sensitivity from these duplicates.

Requires a controlled comparison.
Prefer the clarity argument; do not claim demonstrated FDR harm.
